course.title: Statistical Inference by Simulation
course.tagline: Answer a manager's question with an estimate, an interval, a test and an effect size, each computed by simulation and checked against a known truth
course.description: Participants learn inference by computing it. On synthetic data from a fictional water utility whose true population is known, they draw repeated samples, build bootstrap intervals, run permutation tests beside classical ones, and report effect sizes with intervals instead of bare p-values. They see how testing 30 districts at once produces false findings and correct for it, then fit and read a first linear regression.
course.audience: Practitioners. Graduates and early-career analysts who have completed the FN courses or passed the placement test, and analysts moving into data science.
prerequisites: FN-101 Python for Data and AI Work
FN-103 Mathematics for Machine Learning: Vectors, Gradients and Probability
Filters and groups a table with a dataframe library
Computes a mean, a standard deviation and a simple probability
Pre-work: about two hours on sampling and plotting, labs/P0_prework_sampling_plotting.ipynb, before the supervised entry quiz
Setup: a laptop with uv, or Google Colab. Nothing calls or downloads a model. Run 00_setup_check before Day 1; see labs/README.md.
course.format_note: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task

outcomes.text: Explain what a sampling distribution, a standard error, a confidence interval and a p-value describe, and identify common misreadings, given eight statements from utility reports
outcomes.evidence: a marked sheet with reasons, at least six of eight correct

outcomes.text: Compute bootstrap intervals for a mean, a median and a group difference, resampling the correct unit, given skewed repair times with the population known
outcomes.evidence: each interval with its coverage over 1,000 simulated samples

outcomes.text: Implement a permutation test, compare it with the matching classical test and report an effect size with an interval, given satisfaction scores for two contractors
outcomes.evidence: a script reporting both p-values and the effect size

outcomes.text: Apply family-wise and false discovery rate corrections to many tests and measure the false findings without them, given 30 districts of unequal size, five with a planted difference
outcomes.evidence: true and false discoveries under no correction, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg

outcomes.text: Analyse a linear regression of water consumption on household size and temperature, with slope intervals and residual checks, given 2,000 synthetic metered households
outcomes.evidence: a regression summary, a residual plot and a two-sentence interpretation

outcomes.text: Deliver an inference brief that answers a manager's question with an estimate, an interval, a test, an effect size and stated limits, given a question and a dataset not seen in class
outcomes.evidence: a two-page brief and a notebook that reruns from raw data, defended live

case_study.name: Zulal Water Utility
case_study.summary: Zulal Water Utility (مرفق زلال للمياه) is a fictional regional water utility whose whole population is on file: 80,000 metered households, 12,000 leak repairs by two contractors, 9,000 survey responses and 30 districts of unequal size, all synthetic and generated with a fixed seed. Because the truth is known, every interval and test in the labs is checked against it: repair times are skewed and hold twelve tickets left open for weeks, the survey has a district effect, five districts truly differ in repair time, and larger households live in hotter districts. Participants work as Shadin Al-Qaisi, a junior analyst answering questions from Jamila Al-Shuraim, head of customer operations; household keys are pseudonyms and results are reported by district only.

days.label: Capstone
days.title: Capstone: the inference brief and its defence
days.subtitle: Each participant defends one result of a brief on an unseen question in eight minutes, then answers questions for four

capstone.summary: An inference brief on one of three synthetic questions or an approved public dataset, in a public repository whose README reports estimates, intervals, tests, effect sizes and a coverage check; eight-minute defence plus questions
capstone.submission: A link to a public GitHub repository with a two-page brief, a notebook that reruns from the raw data with a fixed seed, and a README that reports the estimates, intervals, tests, effect sizes and a coverage check, with the commit history and the seeded run log. Then an eight-minute live defence of one result and four minutes of questions, in which the assessor names a different resampling unit and the participant predicts, then shows, the effect.
